statement: Jug A holds 3 litres of a drink that is 40% juice. Jug B holds 4 litres of a drink that is 90% juice. Drink is poured from B into A until the drink in A is 60% juice. Then 1 litre is poured from A back into B. What percentage of the drink in B is now juice?

choices.misconception: I just averaged the two strengths, 90% and 60%, without considering how much of each is in jug B.
I forgot that 2 litres had already left jug B, so I added the returned litre to the full 4 litres.
I added up the juice in jug B correctly but divided by the original 4 litres instead of the 3 litres now in it.
I swapped the weights and mixed one part at 90% with two parts at 60%.

hints: First work out how much drink was poured from B into A.
Track litres of juice, not percentages. After the first pour, find jug A's volume and juice; then follow the litre poured back and recount the juice and the volume in jug B.
Pouring $x$ litres gives $1.2 + 0.9x = 0.6(3 + x)$, so $x = 2$, and jug B is left with 2 litres of its 90% drink.

solutions.reliable: Jug A starts with $0.4 \times 3 = 1.2$ litres of juice. Pouring $x$ litres from B adds $0.9x$ litres of juice, so $1.2 + 0.9x = 0.6(3 + x)$, which gives $0.3x = 0.6$ and $x = 2$. Jug B now holds 2 litres containing 1.8 litres of juice. One litre of A's 60% drink adds 0.6 litres of juice, so B holds 3 litres containing 2.4 litres of juice, and $2.4 \div 3 = 0.8$, which is 80%. The transferable idea: in mixture problems, follow the amount of the ingredient, not the percentage.
solutions.elegant: Jug B ends with 2 litres at 90% and 1 litre at 60%. Its strength is a weighted average, two thirds of the way from 60 towards 90 because there is twice as much of the 90% drink: $60 + 20 = 80$. The transferable idea: a two-part mixture's strength lies closer to the larger part, in proportion to the amounts.

whyOnTest: Mixture questions test whether you track the actual amount of an ingredient through several pours rather than averaging percentages.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
